title: DMK Signals Conditional Support for Delimitation Bill, Breaking From Congress
excerpt: The party's 30 parliamentary votes could hand the NDA the two-thirds majority it needs, provided the bill guarantees proportional seat increases for southern states.
body:
• The DMK has signaled it may support the delimitation bill if it includes a 50% seat increase for every state, proportional representation protections, and a cap on seat redistribution
  • With 22 Lok Sabha and 8 Rajya Sabha MPs, the DMK's 30 votes could help the NDA reach the two-thirds majority required to pass the constitutional amendment
  • Union Minister Kiren Rijiju met Rahul Gandhi in an attempt to break the parliamentary logjam over the delimitation and FCRA bills
  • Congress has rejected reports of DMK support as "bogus" and insists the opposition alliance remains united against the bill

A Pivotal Shift

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam has signaled a dramatic shift on one of India's most politically charged issues, indicating it could support the Centre's proposed delimitation bill under specific conditions — a move that would isolate Congress and potentially hand the ruling NDA coalition the supermajority it needs to redraw India's electoral map.

The DMK, which holds 22 seats in the Lok Sabha and 8 in the Rajya Sabha, has outlined three key conditions: a 50% seat increase applied proportionally across all states, explicit protections for southern states' representation, and a cap on how seats can be redistributed between regions, according to reports from multiple news outlets.

The Numbers Game

The delimitation bill requires a constitutional amendment, demanding a two-thirds majority in both houses of Parliament. The NDA currently holds 318 seats in the Lok Sabha, falling short of the 360-mark threshold. In the Rajya Sabha, the coalition has 143 members against the 163 required.

The DMK's 30 parliamentary votes would significantly close that gap. Combined with potential support from other unaligned regional parties including the YSRCP and NCP factions, the government could assemble a comfortable majority in both houses — something that appeared impossible when the bill was first introduced and failed to advance earlier this year.

Rijiju's Outreach

The political maneuvering has intensified in the current monsoon session. Union Minister of Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju met Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi in what was described as an effort to break the logjam over both the delimitation and FCRA amendment bills.

Rijiju's appeal was notable for its conciliatory tone. Reports indicate the government has softened its stance in recent weeks, potentially influenced by widespread youth protests that have forced recalibration on several legislative priorities. The meeting is seen as the government's recognition that it cannot pass the bill through numbers alone and needs at least a veneer of cross-party consensus.

Congress Pushes Back

Congress has pushed back sharply against reports of fractures in the opposition alliance. Party spokesperson Jairam Ramesh called news of DMK support "bogus" and dismissed the reports as planted stories designed to undermine opposition unity.

Ramesh said Congress leadership remains in touch with DMK leaders and expressed confidence in united opposition against the bill if presented in Parliament. Congress has maintained that it will not support delimitation without a guarantee on women's reservation — a linked constitutional issue that requires delimitation to take effect.

But the DMK has already taken visible steps to distance itself from Congress, seeking separate seating in Parliament and announcing it will evaluate bills on a case-by-case basis rather than following an opposition bloc position — a significant departure from the INDIA alliance framework.

Why Southern States Are Worried

The core anxiety driving the delimitation debate is straightforward: southern states that have successfully controlled population growth — including Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh — fear losing parliamentary seats to faster-growing northern states like Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in any straightforward reapportionment based on population.

The DMK's insistence on a proportional 50% seat increase for all states is designed to address this concern. Under such a formula, every state's seat count would grow, preserving the current ratio rather than redistributing representation from south to north.

What Comes Next

The monsoon session has 19 sittings scheduled over four weeks, and the government is expected to push multiple marquee bills alongside delimitation, including women's reservation, One Nation One Election, and FCRA reforms. Whether the DMK's conditions can be incorporated into the bill — and whether Congress can hold the remaining opposition together — will determine if India's electoral geography is reshaped for the first time since 1976.
nri_angle: Delimitation directly affects parliamentary representation for states with large diaspora populations, particularly Tamil Nadu and Kerala, and could reshape political power in India for decades.
